_provenance.summary: Parameter values and their justification are documented in the section 'Parameter Values and Their Provenance' of CWD_optimal_control.tex. Every entry below carries a confidence tag in the sibling '_notes' block of its section: [LIT] derived from published CWD data, [DEF] a unit-defining normalization (exact by construction), [CAL] back-solved from a calibration target (a target R0, a target term balance), [GUESS] expert judgement with no supporting citation for this study region.
_provenance.state_units: S, I, R are deer/km^2; W is prion-units/km^2 (see reaction._notes.environmental_shedding_rate for the definition of a prion-unit); all rates are per year.
_provenance.spatial_units: Mesh coordinates are in METRES, in the DEM's CRS (the pipeline reprojects the DEM to a UTM CRS, EPSG:32613 by default; the land-cover raster is sampled at mesh nodes in whatever CRS it arrives in, and is never reprojected). Diffusivities are therefore m^2/yr, while densities and transmission coefficients are expressed per km^2. The two conventions never meet: the transmission terms are pointwise and carry no area integral, and the diffusion term is the only place mesh length units enter.
_provenance.mesh_regeneration_required: diffusion_tensor.isotropy feeds the mmg mesh metric in generate_mesh_and_attributes.py as well as the solver, and land_cover.diffusivity is baked into the mesh bundle as land_cover_diffusivity.npy. Change either and an existing mesh bundle must be regenerated before its effective_parameters.json and its baked arrays reflect the new values. Land cover no longer influences the mesh metric itself; the land-cover squish machinery was removed once the small water carrying capacity made the sharp wave fronts it was added for stop appearing.
_provenance.tag_numerical: A [NUMERICAL] tag marks a parameter that exists for conditioning or discretization rather than to represent anything about deer or prions. Tuning one of these on ecological grounds is a category error; diffusion_tensor.isotropy is the parameter this most often happens to.

_notes.final_time_years: [GUESS] A management planning horizon, not a measured quantity. CWD epizootics take one to three decades to move from introduction to double-digit prevalence, so a 20-year horizon is the shortest window over which a culling policy can be meaningfully evaluated. Cost warning: the control driver stores the full state trajectory and the control field is one value per mesh node per step, so memory and time scale linearly with final_time_years / time_step_years (here 1000 steps). Shorten for smoke tests.
_notes.time_step_years: [LIT] 0.02 yr = 7.3 days, matching the weekly timestep of the stochastic CWD model of Almberg et al. (2011). Accuracy, not stability, is the binding constraint: diffusion is implicit and the W update is exact, so the only explicit rates are the reaction terms, the fastest of which is sigma = 1.93/yr, giving dt*sigma = 0.039 << 1.

_notes._compartment_mapping: Almberg et al. (2011) resolve four host stages: exposed (non-shedding), infectious (shedding, pre-clinical), clinical (shedding), and dead. This model has two infected classes, so their exposed stage maps onto I and their infectious + clinical stages are lumped into R. R is therefore the SHEDDING class, of which the terminal clinical phase is a sub-part; it is not the clinical class alone.
_notes.infection_to_clinical_rate: [LIT] sigma = 1/(exposed period). Almberg et al. (2011): mean exposed (non-shedding) period 27 weeks, range 15-35. 52/27 = 1.926/yr, i.e. a mean latency of 0.52 yr. Range implied by their bounds: 1.49-3.47/yr. PREVIOUS VALUE 13.036/yr was 1/(28 days) - a red fox rabies latency, not a CWD one.
_notes.clinical_removal_rate: [LIT] alpha = 1/(shedding period) = 1/(infectious + clinical). Almberg et al. (2011): mean infectious 36 weeks (25-44) plus mean clinical 17 weeks (1-36), so 53 weeks total and alpha = 52/53 = 0.981/yr. Range implied by their bounds: 0.65-1.95/yr. PREVIOUS VALUE 73/yr was 1/(5 days) - again a rabies value.
_notes.environmental_decay_rate: [LIT] delta = -52*ln(gamma) where gamma is Almberg et al.'s weekly prion survival probability, explored over 0.9481-0.9983, i.e. delta in 0.089-2.77/yr (persistence 0.36-11.3 yr). The baseline 0.5/yr (2-year persistence) is the geometric midpoint of that range and coincides with the >=2-year environmental infectivity demonstrated experimentally in mule deer paddocks by Miller et al. (2004). This is the single most consequential parameter in the model - it is the one Almberg et al. identify as driving prevalence and population decline - so it is the first thing to sweep. PREVIOUS VALUE 0.1/yr (10-year persistence) sat at the extreme persistent end of the published range.
_notes.environmental_shedding_rate: [DEF] rho = 1.0 exactly, by construction: one prion-unit is DEFINED as the quantity shed by one clinically-infectious deer over one year. This is a choice of units, not an estimate - the environmental compartment W has no independently measurable scale, so fixing rho absorbs it and leaves environmental_transmission_rate as the single free environmental parameter. Almberg et al. (2011) instead carry a shedding rate tau = 2 units/week plus a carcass pulse phi = 100 units at death; those units are internal to their model and do not transfer.
_notes.intrinsic_growth_rate: [LIT] r = 0.35/yr, i.e. a finite rate of increase lambda = e^0.35 = 1.42 for an unexploited white-tailed deer herd well below carrying capacity. Consistent with the per-capita birth rate of 0.55/yr used by Almberg et al. (2011) net of unhunted adult mortality of roughly 0.15-0.20/yr. Plausible range 0.25-0.50/yr. PREVIOUS VALUE 1.5/yr implies lambda = 4.5, which no cervid population achieves.
_notes.direct_transmission_rate: [CAL] beta_1 = R0_direct / (K_0 * T_shed), where T_shed = 1/alpha = 1.019 yr is the mean time an animal spends in the shedding class. Setting R0_direct = 1.0 (the direct route alone marginally self-sustaining) gives beta_1 = 0.0981 km^2/(deer*yr). Almberg et al.'s beta_d = 7.5e-7 to 2.5e-5 cannot be transferred directly: it is per-individual in a closed 20000-animal population with no area, so it has different dimensions. Note there is no background mortality in this model, so every infected animal reaches the shedding class and T_shed is simply 1/alpha; a variant carrying a non-CWD mortality mu would use T_shed = 1/(alpha+mu) and multiply by P_shed = sigma/(sigma+mu), which at mu = 0.47 would put beta_1 at 0.1805. Was 80 in the original draft, roughly 800x too large, which drove immediate saturation.
_notes.environmental_transmission_rate: [CAL] beta_2 = R0_env * delta / (K_0 * rho * T_shed), with T_shed = 1/alpha as above. An animal in R deposits rho*T_shed prion-units, each persisting a mean 1/delta years and infecting at beta_2*S. Setting R0_env = 1.0 gives beta_2 = 0.04905 km^2/(prion-unit*yr). Total R0 = R0_direct + R0_env = 2.0, an even split between the two routes, which is the qualitative regime Almberg et al. (2011) identify as the interesting one. The split is the assumption here, not the value - sweep it.
_notes._calibration_identity: beta_1 and beta_2 are the ONLY two parameters back-solved from an assumed R0, and they depend on K_0, alpha, delta and rho. If any of those change, both betas must be rescaled or the epidemic threshold moves as a side effect of an unrelated edit. Concretely: beta_1 = R0_dir*alpha/K_0 and beta_2 = R0_env*delta*alpha/(K_0*rho). This is not hypothetical: an earlier revision added a background mortality mu to I and R without rescaling, which dropped R0 from 2.00 to 1.09, nearly to threshold. If mu is ever reinstated the general forms are beta_1 = R0_dir*(sigma+mu)*(alpha+mu)/(sigma*K_0) and beta_2 = R0_env*delta*(sigma+mu)*(alpha+mu)/(sigma*K_0*rho). See the subsection 'Transmission coefficients beta_1 and beta_2, from a target R0' of the .tex.
_notes._equilibrium_check: At these values the spatially uniform endemic equilibrium is S* = K_0/R0 = 5.0, I* = 0.358, R* = 0.703, N* = 6.06 deer/km^2 - a 39% population decline at 17.5% prevalence, which is in the observed range for a CWD core area. S* = K_0/R0 holds exactly and is the check to run after any recalibration.
_notes._no_background_mortality: DELIBERATE OMISSION: there is no non-CWD mortality term on I or R. sigma is the only exit from I and alpha the only exit from R, so every infected deer reaches the shedding class with probability 1 and alpha absorbs disease mortality together with any predation or harvest that targets symptomatic animals. Two consequences worth keeping in view. (i) The model contains no harvest at all, so v = 0 is an unmanaged herd rather than a status-quo managed one, and the control v is total removal effort rather than effort above a normal hunt. (ii) The optimizer sees every culled animal as a certain future shedder, with no chance that something else would have removed it first, which overstates the marginal value of culling. To reinstate mu: add the key back, add -mu*I and -mu*R to the reaction rows and the matching diagonal entries to the adjoint, and rescale both betas by the general formulas in _calibration_identity. Almberg et al. (2011) support mu = -52*ln(0.991) = 0.470/yr for a hunted herd, or roughly 0.20 for an unhunted one.

_notes._control_target: The control acts on R, the SHEDDING class, entering its equation as -v*R; the running cost likewise weights R, not I. This is the right target because R is what drives BOTH transmission routes - directly through beta_1*S*R and indirectly by generating W through rho*R - whereas culling I only delays the same animals' arrival in R. An earlier revision culled I and costed I; the key names changed with it ('cost_infected' became 'cost_shedding'), and shared_parameters.py raises an explicit error on the old key rather than silently substituting a default. MODELLING CAVEAT: R lumps pre-clinical shedders (about 36 weeks, indistinguishable from healthy deer in the field) with clinical animals (about 17 weeks, visibly sick). A control acting on all of R therefore presupposes test-and-cull or some other means of detecting pre-clinical infection; a sight-based cull would reach only the clinical fraction, which is roughly a third of R.
_notes.control_maximum: [GUESS] v_max = 1.0/yr. The control is a per-capita removal rate on R, so v = 1.0 sustained for a year removes 1 - e^-1 = 63% of the shedding class. That is at or beyond the ceiling of any real sharpshooting or agency-cull program; the most intensive Wisconsin CWD-zone efforts did not sustain removal rates of that order landscape-wide. Because the model carries no background mortality and hence no harvest (see reaction._notes._no_background_mortality), v is total removal effort on the shedding class rather than effort above a normal hunt, and v = 0 is an unmanaged herd. PREVIOUS VALUE 5.0/yr implies 99.3% annual removal, which made the box constraint effectively inactive and let the optimizer buy an unrealistically cheap solution.
_notes.cost_shedding: [GUESS] Fixed at 1.0 as the numeraire. Weights R, the shedding class. Only the ratios c1:c2:c3 matter, since scaling J by a positive constant leaves the minimizer unchanged.
_notes.cost_environment: [GUESS] c2 = 0.5. Chosen by the balance recipe in the 'Choosing the weights' subsection of the .tex: at quasi-equilibrium W = rho*R/delta = 2*R exactly, so a unit weight on W would give the environmental term twice the leverage of the shedding term for the same underlying burden. c2 = 0.5 puts the two on equal footing. Recalibrate against a real valuation of landscape contamination.
_notes.cost_control: [GUESS] c3 = 2.0. Chosen so that c3*v^2 at half effort (v = 0.5) is comparable to c1*R at the scale of the endemic shedding density R* = 0.70 deer/km^2: 2.0*0.25 = 0.5 against 0.70, i.e. the two terms sit within a factor of 1.4, which is what 'comparable' has to mean here. Without a weight of roughly this size the quadratic penalty is negligible against the state terms and the optimizer simply pins v at v_max everywhere. Was 4.0 when the cost weighted I, whose endemic density is of order 1 deer/km^2. This is the weight most in need of replacement by an actual per-deer cull cost set against an actual valuation of a shedding deer.
_notes.cost_control_l1: [GUESS] c4 = 0.0 by default, which reproduces the pure-quadratic objective exactly; this key is opt-in. Setting it positive adds an L1 (elastic-net) term c4*v to the running cost, moving stationarity from v* = P[lambda_R*R/(2*c3)] to v* = P[(lambda_R*R - c4)/(2*c3)]. The practical effect is a THRESHOLD: the optimum is exactly zero wherever lambda_R*R < c4, instead of the quadratic penalty's whisper of effort spread over the whole domain (a 5-year example run put peak effort at 0.042/yr and the space-time mean at 0.0045/yr - nominally 'cull everywhere, barely'). That is the 'not here' half of a cull-here-not-there map, and it is the half a management plan actually needs. NOT a nonsmooth term despite the name: because v >= 0 is already imposed, int|v| = int v on the admissible set, so the kink of the absolute value sits exactly on the constraint boundary and the objective stays smooth - L-BFGS-B applies unchanged, with no proximal or FISTA machinery. Do NOT reach for a smoothed surrogate like sqrt(v^2 + eps): its curvature is eps^(-1/2) at the origin and decays like eps/v^3 away from it, a spread of order 1e6 across the box at eps = 1e-6, which manufactures ill-conditioning and is a known way to destroy convergence on this kind of problem. The real cost of raising c4 while lowering c3 is the loss of strong convexity: c3 contributes a uniform 2*c3*I floor to the reduced Hessian, and without it only the compact state-coupling operator remains, whose spectrum decays to zero. c3 -> 0 is the pure bang-bang limit and is where conditioning degrades - a continuous dial, not a cliff. Sweep c4 and watch two numbers: the iteration count and the fraction of the domain at exactly zero.
_notes.initial_step_size: [GUESS] Numerical, not physical. The Armijo search grows and shrinks it adaptively, so it only affects how many backtracks the first iteration takes. Used only by optimizer = 'projected-gradient'.
_notes.control_block_years: [GUESS] 1.0 yr, i.e. the culling effort is held constant within each year and the optimizer chooses one spatial field per year (20 over the default horizon). This is a RESTRICTION OF THE ADMISSIBLE SET, so the optimal J it reaches is no lower than the per-step optimum - but it is a restriction toward realism, not away from it: the per-step alternative lets effort change every 7.3 days, which no agency does, whereas quotas are in fact set annually. It is also what makes a quasi-Newton method affordable. The optimization variable is one CG1 field per block, so on a 210k-node mesh over 1000 steps a per-step control is 1.7 GiB per copy and L-BFGS-B at lbfgs_memory = 10 would need about 39 GiB of correction pairs; annual blocking cuts both by fifty. Set to null to recover one value per time step, which is what this workflow did before blocking existed. Shorten to 0.25 for seasonal structure (e.g. to resolve a hunting season) at four times the cost.
_notes.optimizer: [NUMERICAL] 'lbfgs' runs SciPy's L-BFGS-B on the reduced problem, which handles the box constraint directly and picks up curvature; 'projected-gradient' is the original projected steepest descent with an Armijo line search. Both consume the identical adjoint gradient, so --gradient-check validates either. Projected gradient converges linearly at a rate set by the reduced Hessian's conditioning and is retained mainly as a reference implementation and a fallback when SciPy is unavailable.
_notes.lbfgs_memory: [NUMERICAL] Correction pairs retained by L-BFGS-B (SciPy's 'maxcor'). Peak memory is roughly (2*lbfgs_memory + 5) control-sized arrays, so it trades directly against control_block_years: at annual blocking on a 210k-node mesh one array is 34 MiB and the default 10 costs under a gigabyte. Lower it before lowering the block length if memory binds.
_notes._tolerances: gradient_tolerance and relative_cost_tolerance are absolute numbers compared against quantities whose scale depends on the mesh area and the state magnitudes. After the rescaling in this revision they may be unreachably tight or trivially loose; check the printed optimization history and adjust rather than trusting 1e-8.

_notes.mean: [CAL] Amplitude chosen so each focus integrates to exactly one introduced infected animal. For an isotropic Gaussian of amplitude m and standard deviation s, the integral is 2*pi*s^2*m; with s = 500 m = 0.5 km this gives m = 1/(2*pi*0.25) = 0.637 deer/km^2. PREVIOUS VALUE 0.01 corresponded to 1/64 of a deer per focus - numerically harmless but not interpretable as an index case.
_notes.standard_deviation: [GUESS] 500 m, chosen as roughly the linear scale of a white-tailed deer home range (about 1-3 km^2), i.e. the area over which a single index case actually deposits prions and makes contacts.
_notes.center: [GUESS] Placement is arbitrary and mesh-dependent; these coordinates are offsets from the mesh centroid recorded in coord_offsets.npy. Replace with actual first-detection locations for the study region.

_notes._what_this_is: Before any infection is seeded, the S equation is run on its own (I = R = W = 0) from S = K until it stops moving, and the relaxed field is cached in the mesh bundle as susceptible_equilibrium.npy for every later run to start from. K is a piecewise-constant land-cover lookup and is NOT a steady state of the S equation: diffusion smooths it across every patch boundary, and water (K = 0, where growth becomes -r*S) is an absorbing sink that draws the profile down for a diffusion length around every shoreline. Starting at S = K therefore lays an order-one demographic transient on top of the epidemic one, and at r = 0.35/yr the two relax on comparable timescales, so it does not wash out before the interesting dynamics begin. For the control problem it is worse than cosmetic: the spurious structure is something the optimizer will spend effort on. The cache is keyed by a signature of the mesh geometry, both nodal data arrays, and the parameters below, so changing the mesh, the land cover, kappa, or r recomputes it instead of silently reusing a stale field.
_notes.enabled: [NUMERICAL] Set false to start S at the raw carrying capacity, which is what this workflow did before the spin-up existed. Useful only for reproducing older runs.
_notes.max_duration_years: [NUMERICAL] 60 yr, a CAP rather than a target: the solve exits as soon as drift_tolerance is met, which normally happens long before. Two processes have to finish, and the slower one sets the requirement. Logistic relaxation is the fast one, with an e-folding time 1/r = 2.9 yr. Diffusive smoothing is the slow one: at kappa = 4 km^2/yr, equilibrating across a patch of linear scale L takes of order L^2/kappa, which is 1 yr for a 2 km patch but 25 yr for a 10 km one, and shoreline drawdown around a large lake is slower still. A couple of years is therefore NOT enough - it leaves roughly a third of the initial deviation - which is why this is a convergence-based stop with a generous ceiling rather than a fixed short run. Overshooting costs one scalar solve; stopping early contaminates every simulation built on the cached field.
_notes.time_step_years: [NUMERICAL] null means reuse time.time_step_years (0.02 yr). Accuracy, not stability, is the constraint here as in the main solve: diffusion is implicit and the only explicit rate is r = 0.35/yr, so dt*r = 0.007. A larger step would make the spin-up cheaper, but the implicit Euler diffusion is only first-order in time and a coarse step biases the smoothed profile it is meant to resolve. Raise it only if the spin-up is a noticeable share of run time.
_notes.drift_tolerance: [NUMERICAL] Stop when max|dS/dt| over the mesh falls below this fraction of peak K per year - a relative measure, so it is independent of the density units. At 1e-5 and K_0 = 10 deer/km^2 the field is moving by under 1e-4 deer/km^2/yr, i.e. under a five-hundredth of a deer per km^2 across the entire 20-year horizon: negligible against every other error in the model. Loosening it to 1e-3 saves time but leaves a visible residual drift in long runs.

_notes._units: m^2/yr, because mesh coordinates are metres. kappa now carries the ENTIRE physical magnitude and compartment_scales are dimensionless mobility ratios. Previously the magnitude was split arbitrarily between kappa = 200 and compartment_scales = 100.
_notes.kappa: [GUESS] 4.0e6 m^2/yr = 4 km^2/yr on flat, maximally permeable land cover. Two independent order-of-magnitude arguments bracket it. (i) Dispersal: roughly a quarter of white-tailed deer disperse once as yearlings over a median of order 8-10 km; spreading that mean squared displacement over a population turnover time of a few years gives D of order 3 km^2/yr. (ii) Front speed: a Fisher-KPP invasion advances at c = 2*sqrt(D*r_I), so an observed CWD front speed of a few km/yr with an infection growth rate r_I of order 0.3/yr implies D of order 5-8 km^2/yr. Both land in the 2-8 km^2/yr band. NOT backed by a fitted estimate from any single paper - this is the least defensible of the reaction-diffusion parameters and the wave speed is proportional to sqrt(kappa), so a factor-of-4 error is only a factor-of-2 error in spread rate.
_notes.isotropy: [NUMERICAL] 0.02. NOT a movement parameter - do not tune it as one. The slope physics lives entirely in the activation function: Ds = kappa*(isotropy + (1-isotropy)*activation) equals kappa on flat ground and falls toward the floor as terrain steepens, with activation_cosine_threshold and activation_steepness setting where and how sharply. All isotropy does is stop Ds reaching zero, which would drop the tangent-plane tensor from rank 2 to rank 1, leave the stiffness matrix singular along the downhill direction e_s, and blow up the 1/r mmg mesh metric. It is a degeneracy floor, so it wants to be small enough not to interfere with the activation function but large enough to keep the tensor conditioned - 0.02 gives a tangent-plane condition number of 50. It also sets the mesh floor hmin = isotropy * hmax = 3 m. A revision of this file briefly raised it to 0.1 on the mistaken reasoning that 50:1 anisotropy on steep ground was ecologically implausible; strong anisotropy there is exactly what the activation function is meant to produce.
_notes.activation_cosine_threshold: [GUESS] 0.96, i.e. the slope at which mobility is half-suppressed is acos(0.96) = 16.3 degrees. Chosen to sit inside the 15-25 degree band above which cervid habitat-selection studies generally show avoidance. No CWD-specific source.
_notes.activation_steepness: [GUESS] 50, in units of inverse cosine. The transition spans roughly cos(theta) from 0.92 to 1.0, i.e. slopes of 0-23 degrees. Purely a smoothness choice - it controls how abruptly mobility falls off, not where.
_notes.compartment_scales: [GUESS] S and I at 1.0: sub-clinical infected deer are not detectably less mobile than susceptibles. R (code name 'dying') at 0.3: clinically affected deer show markedly contracted movement in the terminal phase. Because R is a lumped pre-clinical-plus-clinical shedding class (see reaction._notes._compartment_mapping), 0.3 is a blend of near-normal and near-zero mobility rather than a clinical-stage value. PREVIOUS VALUE had all three equal at 100.0, i.e. no differential mobility at all.

_notes.carrying_capacity_base: [GUESS] K_0 = 10 deer/km^2 (about 26 deer/mi^2) in the best habitat class, giving a landscape mean of roughly 6-8 deer/km^2 once the fractions below are applied. This is a high but attainable density for a Midwestern or eastern white-tailed deer herd. It is REGION-SPECIFIC and should be replaced with the state agency's overwinter density estimate for the actual study area. PREVIOUS VALUE 2.0 deer/km^2 is a boreal or heavily-hunted-herd density, roughly five times too low for the habitat this model is aimed at. Note that beta_1 and beta_2 were back-solved from this value (see reaction._notes._calibration_identity) and must be rescaled if it changes.
_notes._two_tables_measure_different_things: carrying_capacity_fractions measures HABITAT QUALITY (how many deer a cover type supports); diffusivity measures PERMEABILITY (how readily deer move through it). These are anti-correlated for several classes and must not be collapsed into one table. Open grassland is highly permeable but poor habitat - deer cross it quickly and do not linger. Woody wetlands are prime cover and browse but slow to move through. The previous file had grassland at the top of BOTH tables and woody wetlands near the bottom of both, which is backwards for white-tailed deer on the habitat side.
_notes.carrying_capacity_fractions: [GUESS] Expert judgement from white-tailed deer habitat ecology; no fitted source. Deciduous and mixed forest and their edges rank highest (1.0, 0.95); woody wetlands are prime cover and winter browse (0.9, RAISED from 0.35); developed open space - parks, golf courses, exurban lawn-and-woodlot mosaic - supports famously high suburban deer densities (0.9); shrub/scrub is excellent browse (0.85); cropland and pasture provide seasonal forage but no cover, so they depend on adjacent edge (0.75, 0.7); pure grassland offers little browse and no cover (0.5, LOWERED from 1.0); evergreen stands are poor forage but important thermal cover (0.6); barren rock and sand support almost nothing (0.1, LOWERED from 0.4); ice and snow and open water are zero. Calibrate against regional density estimates stratified by cover type.
_notes.diffusivity: [GUESS] Expert judgement; no fitted source. Values are dimensionless multipliers on kappa, normalized so that the most permeable classes (grassland, pasture) sit at 1.0. Open, unobstructed cover is most permeable; forest and shrub impose moderate resistance; wetlands and dense development impose heavy resistance; high-intensity development is near-impermeable. Open water at 0.01 (RAISED from 0.0001) treats large water bodies as strong but not absolute barriers, since deer do swim - the previous value both overstated the barrier and, because this table drives the mmg mesh metric, forced an extremely fine mesh along every shoreline.
_notes._defaults: diffusivity_default and carrying_capacity_fraction_default apply to class codes absent from the tables above; both LOWERED from 1.0 to 0.5 so that unmapped or nodata cells default to a mid-range value rather than to prime, maximally permeable habitat.
